q: How fast is CO2 in the atmosphere rising?

queries.purpose: Yearly rise in atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa, last 30 years
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(co2_ppm - LAG(co2_ppm) OVER (ORDER BY year), 2) AS value FROM co2_annual QUALIFY year >= (SELECT MAX(year) FROM co2_annual) - 29 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average yearly rise in CO2 by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(decade AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(diff), 2) AS value FROM (SELECT year, FLOOR(year/10)*10 AS decade, co2_ppm - LAG(co2_ppm) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS diff FROM co2_annual) WHERE diff IS NOT NULL GROUP BY decade ORDER BY decade LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Annual mean CO2 level, every 5 years
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(co2_ppm, 1) AS value FROM co2_annual WHERE year % 5 = 0 OR year = (SELECT MAX(year) FROM co2_annual) ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

story.lead: CO2 in the air is rising faster than ever
story.summary: Carbon dioxide in the air at Mauna Loa rose by **2.74 ppm** in 2025, and by **3.53 ppm** in 2024. In the 1960s it rose by under **1 ppm** a year on average, so the yearly rise is now about three times as big. The level hit **427.4 ppm** in 2025, up from **316.9 ppm** in 1960.
story.sub: NOAA yearly averages at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, 1959–2025. ppm means parts per million: CO2 molecules per million air molecules.

facts.label: rise in 2025, the latest full year
CO2 level in 2025, up from 316.9 in 1960

points.h: Every recent year added more than 1 ppm
points.p: The yearly rise bounces around, from **1.14 ppm** in 1997 to **3.53 ppm** in 2024. It has never been negative in this period. The last ten years have mostly been higher than the 1990s.

points.h: Each decade has brought a bigger yearly rise
points.p: The average yearly rise grew from **0.86 ppm** in the 1960s to **1.91 ppm** in the 2000s. In the 2020s so far it is **2.62 ppm** a year. The only small dip was in the 1990s, at **1.53 ppm**, just below the 1980s.

points.h: The CO2 level has climbed steadily since 1960
points.p: The yearly average went from **316.9 ppm** in 1960 to **427.4 ppm** in 2025, a gain of about **110 ppm**. Over the first 25 years it rose about 30 ppm, from 1960 to 1985. In the last 25 years it rose about 47 ppm, from 2000 to 2025.

story.note: These are measurements from one site in Hawaii, shown as yearly averages. The 2020s figure covers only the years up to 2025.

q: Which countries have the biggest economies?

queries.purpose: Top 15 economies by GDP in 2023 (current US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, round(gdp_usd/1e12, 2) AS value FROM gdp WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2023 AND gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY gdp_usd DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 15 economies by GDP per person in 2023 among countries with over 10 million people
queries.sql: SELECT g.country AS label, round(g.gdp_usd/p.population) AS value FROM gdp g JOIN population p ON g.country_code = p.country_code AND g.year = p.year WHERE NOT g.is_aggregate AND g.year = 2023 AND g.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL AND p.population > 10000000 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 10 economies by GDP in 2000 for comparison (current US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, round(gdp_usd/1e12, 2) AS value FROM gdp WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2000 AND gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY gdp_usd DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: The US and China have by far the biggest economies.
story.summary: In 2023 the United States produced **$27.36 trillion** of goods and services, and China **$17.79 trillion**. Together that is more than the next thirteen countries on the list added up... roughly, the third-placed Germany is at only **$4.46 trillion**, about a quarter of China's size. Both figures are in current US dollars.
story.sub: World Bank GDP and population, 2023, with 2000 for comparison; current US dollars, countries only (no regions or groups).

facts.label: US economy in 2023, the world's largest

points.h: The US and China are far ahead of everyone else
points.p: The US leads at **$27.36 trillion**, with China second at **$17.79 trillion**. Germany is third at **$4.46 trillion**, so the gap between second and third is huge. India (**$3.55 trillion**) is fifth, ahead of the UK and France.

points.h: Rich per person: the US leads, China is not on the list
points.p: Dividing each economy by its population, the US comes first at **$81,249** per person, ahead of Australia at **$64,660**. China and India do not make the top 15 here, though they are among the biggest economies overall. This list only includes countries with more than 10 million people.

points.h: In 2000, China was only sixth
points.p: In 2000 the US was already first at **$10.25 trillion**, and Japan second at **$4.97 trillion**. China was sixth at **$1.21 trillion**. By 2023 China had grown to about **15 times** that size, while Japan's economy had slipped to fourth place at $4.21 trillion.

story.note: GDP is measured in current US dollars, so the growth since 2000 includes rising prices and exchange-rate changes, not only more output.

Which countries have grown fastest since 2000?
How do India's and Japan's economies compare over time?

q: How much has the world warmed?

queries.purpose: Global temperature anomaly by decade (NASA GISTEMP, above the 1951-1980 average)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(CAST(floor(year/10)*10 AS INTEGER) AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, round(avg(anomaly_c), 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' GROUP BY floor(year/10) ORDER BY floor(year/10)

queries.purpose: Yearly anomaly over the last 30 years (NASA GISTEMP)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(anomaly_c, 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' AND year >= (SELECT max(year) - 29 FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP') ORDER BY year

queries.purpose: Ten warmest years on record (NASA GISTEMP)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(anomaly_c, 2) AS value FROM temperature WHERE source = 'GISTEMP' ORDER BY anomaly_c DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: The world is about 1.2°C warmer than 1951–1980.
story.summary: NASA's record shows 2025 was **1.19°C** above the 1951–1980 average. The 2020s so far average **1.07°C** above it, compared with **-0.22°C** in the 1880s. That is a gap of about **1.3°C** between the first and latest decade on record.
story.sub: NASA GISTEMP global surface temperature, 1880–2025, compared with the 1951–1980 average.

points.h: Each decade has been warmer than the one before since the 1970s
points.p: Decades in the 1880s to 1910s sat below the 1951–1980 average, at about **-0.22°C** to **-0.34°C**. Since the 1970s (**0.03°C**), every decade has been warmer, reaching **1.07°C** in the 2020s so far. The 2020s average is about **0.26°C** above the 2010s.

points.h: Recent years have climbed from about 0.4°C to over 1°C
points.p: In 1996 the world was **0.33°C** above the 1951–1980 average. Since 2015, every year has been at least **0.85°C** above it. The last three years were **1.17°C**, **1.29°C** and **1.19°C**.

points.h: The ten warmest years are all from 2015 onward
points.p: All ten of the warmest years on record fall between 2015 and 2025. The top three are the latest three years: 2024 (**1.29°C**), 2025 (**1.19°C**) and 2023 (**1.17°C**). Even the tenth warmest, 2018, was **0.85°C** above the average.

story.note: These are degrees Celsius above NASA's 1951–1980 average, not above the 1800s, so the numbers are not directly comparable with other baselines.

q: How much have US house prices risen?

queries.purpose: US national home price index by year (January 2000 = 100), annual average
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG("index"), 1) AS value FROM us_house_prices WHERE area = 'US national' AND year(month) < 2026 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Percent rise in home prices since Jan 1987 vs latest month, by metro and national
queries.sql: WITH f AS (SELECT area, arg_min("index", month) AS first_v, arg_max("index", month) AS last_v FROM us_house_prices WHERE area NOT IN ('20-city composite','10-city composite') GROUP BY area) SELECT regexp_replace(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, ROUND((last_v / first_v - 1) * 100, 0) AS value FROM f ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: US national index at January each year since 2000 vs January 2000 base
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND("index", 1) AS value FROM us_house_prices WHERE area = 'US national' AND month(month) = 1 AND year(month) >= 2000 ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

story.lead: US house prices are up about 429% since 1987
story.summary: The national home price index is about **429%** higher than in January 1987, so homes cost roughly five times as much. Since January 2000 the index has gone from 100 to **326.8** in January 2026, more than three times. The climb was not smooth: prices fell about a quarter after 2007 before rising again.
story.sub: S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller home price index, US national and metro areas, 1987 to July 2026 (not adjusted for inflation).

points.h: Prices climbed, then fell after 2006, then recovered
points.p: The yearly average index rose from **66.3** in 1987 to a peak of **183.5** in 2006. It then slid to **139.2** by 2011. By 2016 it was back up to **180.9**, almost at the old peak. This chart only shows 1987 to 2016.

points.h: West Coast cities gained most; Dallas gained least
points.p: San Diego (**724%**), Portland (**714%**) and San Francisco (**696%**) rose the most. The US as a whole rose **429%**. Dallas rose the least, at **197%**. Some cities start later than 1987, so each city is measured from its own first month, and Dallas from 2000.

points.h: Since 2000 prices have more than tripled
points.p: The index started at **100** in January 2000 and reached **326.8** in January 2026. It dipped to **134.2** in 2012, then rose steadily. From January 2020 to January 2022 it jumped from **212.4** to **281.9**, about a third in two years.

story.note: These are prices in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so part of the rise is just general price growth.

Which US cities had the biggest drop in prices after 2006?

q: How have oil prices changed since 2000?

queries.purpose: Average Brent crude price per year since 2000
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_barrel), 1) AS value FROM oil_prices WHERE benchmark = 'Brent' AND year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Highest monthly Brent price in each year since 2000
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(MAX(usd_per_barrel), 1) AS value FROM oil_prices WHERE benchmark = 'Brent' AND year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average WTI price per year since 2000, for comparison with Brent
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_barrel), 1) AS value FROM oil_prices WHERE benchmark = 'WTI' AND year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

story.lead: Oil prices roughly tripled since 2000, with big swings.
story.summary: Brent crude averaged **$28.5** a barrel in 2000 and **$90.6** so far in 2026, about three times as much. The path was bumpy: prices peaked near **$112** in 2011–2012, then fell to **$43.5** in 2016. These are current dollars, so part of the rise is general price growth.
story.sub: Monthly Brent and WTI crude oil spot prices (US EIA), 2000 to 2026, in nominal US dollars per barrel; 2026 is a partial year.

facts.label: Average Brent price per barrel, 2000 vs 2026 so far
Highest monthly Brent price so far in 2026

points.h: Brent averaged about $25–29 in the early 2000s, then climbed
points.p: The yearly average rose from **$28.5** in 2000 to **$111.7** in 2012. It then fell to **$43.5** in 2016, rose to **$100.8** in 2022, and was **$90.6** so far in 2026. In 2020 it dropped to **$41.8**.

points.h: Monthly peaks show even sharper spikes than yearly averages
points.p: The highest single month was **$132.7** in 2008, well above that year's average of $96.8. The 2026 peak so far is **$117.3**, far above the 2025 peak of **$79.3**. Yearly averages hide how high prices got within a year.

points.h: US benchmark WTI followed Brent, usually a little lower
points.p: WTI averaged **$30.3** in 2000 and **$83.4** so far in 2026. In most years it sat a few dollars below Brent; in 2026 so far, **$83.4** against **$90.6**. The ups and downs are nearly identical.

story.note: Prices are in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and 2026 covers only part of the year.

q: Is the sea level rising faster?

queries.purpose: Pace of rise per decade, tide-gauge reconstruction (CSIRO), 1880s-2000s
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, round(regr_slope(csiro_inches, year) * 10, 2) AS value FROM sea_level WHERE csiro_inches IS NOT NULL AND year <= 2009 GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10

queries.purpose: Pace of rise in the satellite era (NOAA), by period
queries.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN year <= 2002 THEN '1993-2002' WHEN year <= 2012 THEN '2003-2012' ELSE '2013-2023' END AS label, round(regr_slope(noaa_inches, year) * 10, 2) AS value FROM sea_level WHERE noaa_inches IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY min(year)

queries.purpose: Total rise since 1880 at the start of each decade (CSIRO)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(csiro_inches, 2) AS value FROM sea_level WHERE csiro_inches IS NOT NULL AND year % 10 = 0 ORDER BY year

story.lead: Yes, sea level is rising faster lately.
story.summary: Sea level has gone up about **8.8 inches** since 1880, and the pace has picked up. Tide gauges show **1.45 inches** per decade in the 2000s, the fastest of any decade since 1880. Satellites show **1.54 inches** per decade in 2013-2023, up from **0.96** in 2003-2012.
story.sub: Global average sea level, US EPA: tide-gauge reconstruction (CSIRO) 1880-2013 and satellite readings (NOAA) 1993-2023.

facts.label: rise per decade in the 2000s (tide gauges)

points.h: Tide gauges: the 2000s were the fastest decade
points.p: Early decades bounced around, from nearly flat (**-0.03** inches in the 1900s) to about **0.8** inches per decade. The 2000s stand out at **1.45 inches** per decade, nearly twice the 1990s pace of **0.85**.

points.h: Satellites: the latest decade is the fastest
points.p: Satellites show a rise of **1.06** inches per decade in 1993-2002 and **0.96** in 2003-2012. In 2013-2023 it jumped to **1.54** inches per decade, about **60%** faster than the decade before.

points.h: Total rise since 1880 keeps climbing, and steepens
points.p: By 2010 the sea was **8.83 inches** higher than in 1880. Over the last two decades alone it added about **2.6 inches** (from 6.25 in 1990 to 8.83 in 2010). That is roughly the same as the whole rise from 1880 to 1930, which was about 2 inches.

story.note: The two sources use different baselines and cover different years, so compare the pace within each, not the totals between them.

q: What is the US unemployment rate over time?

queries.purpose: US unemployment rate by year, 1947-2025 (annual average, % of labour force)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(unemployment_rate_pct, 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1947 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30 OFFSET 0

queries.purpose: Average US unemployment rate by decade (percent of labour force)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(unemployment_rate_pct), 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1950 GROUP BY (year // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Share of the population with a job (employment-population ratio), by decade average
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(employment_population_ratio_pct), 1) AS value FROM us_employment WHERE year >= 1950 GROUP BY (year // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

story.lead: US unemployment rises in downturns, then falls back
story.summary: The share of US workers without a job has swung between about **3%** and **8.5%** in the years shown from 1947 to 1976. Decade averages peaked at **7.3%** in the 1980s and are **4.8%** in the 2020s so far. That means roughly one in 14 people looking for work in the 1980s went without a job, against about one in 21 now.
story.sub: US Bureau of Labor Statistics yearly averages. The yearly chart shows 1947–1976 only; the decade charts cover 1950–2025.

facts.label: Average rate in the 1980s, the highest decade

points.h: Unemployment jumped in bad years, then eased, 1947–1976
points.p: Between 1947 and 1976 the rate hovered mostly between 3% and 6%. It jumped in some years, such as **5.9%** in 1949, **6.8%** in 1958 and **8.5%** in 1975. The low point was **2.9%** in 1953. This chart stops at 1976, so later years are not shown.

points.h: The 1980s had the highest average unemployment
points.p: The average rate climbed from **4.5%** in the 1950s to **7.3%** in the 1980s. It then dropped to **5.5%** in the 2000s. The 2010s averaged **6.2%**. The 2020s, covering 2020 to 2025, average **4.8%**, about the same as the 1960s.

points.h: A smaller share of people have jobs than in the 1990s
points.p: The share of all adults with a job rose from **56.6%** in the 1950s to **62.8%** in the 1990s. It has since fallen to **59.2%** in the 2020s. So the 2020s have lower unemployment than the 2010s, but the share of people in work is about the same, at roughly **59%**.

story.note: The unemployment rate counts only people looking for work; the 2020s figures cover 2020–2025 only.

q: How much has gold gone up?

queries.purpose: Gold price by decade (average, nominal US dollars per ounce)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year(month) // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_ounce), 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) >= 1900 GROUP BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average gold price per year since 2000 (nominal US dollars, 2026 so far)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_ounce), 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) >= 2000 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Gold price at the start of selected years vs latest month (nominal US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(usd_per_ounce, 0) AS value FROM gold_prices WHERE (month IN (SELECT MIN(month) FROM gold_prices WHERE year(month) IN (1900,1925,1950,1971,1980,2000,2010,2020) GROUP BY year(month))) OR month = (SELECT MAX(month) FROM gold_prices) ORDER BY month LIMIT 30

story.lead: Gold is now about 225 times its 1900 price
story.summary: An ounce of gold cost about **$19** in January 1900 and **$4,319** in September 2026. That is roughly **225 times** as much, in current dollars. Most of the rise came after 1971, and the price has more than doubled since 2023.
story.sub: Monthly gold prices in nominal US dollars per troy ounce, January 1900 to September 2026 (2026 so far).

facts.label: Price per ounce, Jan 1900 to Sep 2026

points.h: Gold stayed cheap for decades, then jumped from the 1970s
points.p: The average price sat between **$19** and **$36** an ounce from the 1900s through the 1960s. In the 1970s it jumped to **$132**, and in the 2020s so far it averages **$2,453**.

points.h: The price has climbed steeply since 2023
points.p: Yearly averages rose from **$279** in 2000 to **$1,670** in 2012. They then slipped to **$1,161** in 2015. Since 2023 the average has risen from **$1,943** to **$4,552** in 2026 so far, more than double.

points.h: Starting prices show how big the rise has been
points.p: Gold was about **$35** in January 1950 and **$38** in January 1971. By January 1980 it was **$675**. The latest month, September 2026, is **$4,319**, which is more than **110 times** the 1971 price.

story.note: These prices are in current US dollars and are not adjusted for inflation, so part of the rise over a century is just general price growth.

How did the gold price change in 2008 and 2020?
How does the gold price compare with oil prices since 1986?

queries.purpose: GDP in 2023 as a multiple of 2000 (current US dollars), economies of at least $10bn in 2000
queries.sql: SELECT g23.country AS label, round(g23.gdp_usd / g00.gdp_usd, 1) AS value FROM gdp g00 JOIN gdp g23 ON g00.country_code = g23.country_code AND g00.year = 2000 AND g23.year = 2023 WHERE NOT g00.is_aggregate AND g00.gdp_usd >= 1e10 AND g23.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Biggest total GDP gain 2000 to 2023 (billions of current US dollars)
queries.sql: SELECT g23.country AS label, round((g23.gdp_usd - g00.gdp_usd) / 1e9) AS value FROM gdp g00 JOIN gdp g23 ON g00.country_code = g23.country_code AND g00.year = 2000 AND g23.year = 2023 WHERE NOT g00.is_aggregate AND g23.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL AND g00.gdp_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Fastest population growth 2000 to 2025 (percent), countries with at least 1 million people in 2000
queries.sql: SELECT p25.country AS label, round((p25.population * 1.0 / p00.population - 1) * 100) AS value FROM population p00 JOIN population p25 ON p00.country_code = p25.country_code AND p00.year = 2000 AND p25.year = 2025 WHERE NOT p00.is_aggregate AND p00.population >= 1000000 AND p25.population IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

story.lead: China, Kazakhstan and Viet Nam grew fastest
story.summary: Measured by the size of their economy, China grew most: it was **14.7 times** larger in 2023 than in 2000, with Kazakhstan (**14.3**) and Viet Nam (**13.8**) close behind. In total dollars added, the United States (**$17.1 trillion**) and China (**$16.6 trillion**) are far ahead of everyone else. All figures are in current US dollars, so they include price rises.
story.sub: World Bank GDP in current US dollars, 2000 vs 2023; population 2000 vs 2025.

points.h: China, Kazakhstan and Viet Nam grew more than 13-fold
points.p: Among economies worth at least $10 billion in 2000, China's output rose **14.7 times**. Kazakhstan (**14.3**) and Viet Nam (**13.8**) are almost level with it. Romania is next at **9.4**, so the top three stand clear of the rest.

points.h: The US and China added the most dollars
points.p: The United States added about **$17.1 trillion** and China about **$16.6 trillion**. India is a distant third at **$3.1 trillion**. China's gain is nearly equal to the US one, even though the US started far larger.

points.h: Gulf and African countries grew their populations fastest
points.p: The United Arab Emirates had the fastest population growth: **230%**, so it has more than three times as many people as in 2000. Kuwait (**149%**), Chad (**147%**) and Niger (**143%**) follow. Many of the top 15 more than doubled in size.

story.note: GDP is in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and the first chart only includes economies of at least $10 billion in 2000.

q: Where does the world's CO2 come from?

queries.purpose: 2024 CO2 emissions by source
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Oil' AS label, ROUND(liquid*3.664/1000, 1) AS value FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Coal', ROUND(solid*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Natural gas', ROUND(gas*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Cement', ROUND(cement*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 'Gas flaring', ROUND(flaring*3.664/1000, 1) FROM co2_emissions WHERE year = 2024) ORDER BY value DESC

queries.purpose: Coal's share of fossil fuel and cement CO2 by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(solid) / SUM(total_mt_carbon), 1) AS value FROM co2_emissions WHERE year >= 1900 GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10

queries.purpose: Average yearly total CO2 emissions by decade (2020s so far = 2020-2024)
queries.unit: billion tonnes of CO2 per year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(total_mt_carbon) * 3.664 / 1000, 1) AS value FROM co2_emissions WHERE year >= 1900 GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10

story.lead: Coal and oil produce most of the world's CO2
story.summary: In 2024, coal gave off **15.8 billion tonnes** of CO2 and oil **12.5 billion tonnes**. Together that is about **28 billion** of the roughly 38 billion tonnes from fossil fuels and cement, or around three-quarters. Natural gas adds **8 billion tonnes**.
story.sub: Global CO2 from fossil fuels and cement, Global Carbon Project; 2024 by source, and decades from 1900 to 2024.

facts.label: CO2 from coal in 2024, the largest source
coal's share of the total in the 2020s so far
average yearly CO2 in the 2020s, so far

points.h: Coal is the biggest source, ahead of oil and gas
points.p: In 2024 coal gave off **15.8 billion tonnes** of CO2, oil **12.5** and natural gas **8**. Cement (**1.5**) and gas flaring (**0.4**) are much smaller. Coal alone is more than the cement, flaring and gas figures combined.

points.h: Coal's share fell from almost all to about 40%
points.p: In the 1900s coal made up **95%** of the total. By the 1970s it was down to **35.2%**, as oil and gas grew. Since then it has crept back up and sits at **40.9%** in the 2020s.

points.h: Yearly emissions are about 15 times higher than in 1900s
points.p: The average was **2.4 billion tonnes** a year in the 1900s and **37.2 billion** in the 2020s. That is roughly **15 times** as much. Growth has slowed lately: the 2020s average is only about 2 billion above the 2010s.

story.note: Figures cover CO2 from fossil fuels and cement only, shown in tonnes of CO2 (not tonnes of carbon); the 2020s cover 2020-2024.

q: How much ice have glaciers lost?

queries.purpose: Cumulative ice lost since 1956, by decade (metres of water equivalent)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(-cumulative_mass_balance_mwe, 1) AS value FROM glaciers WHERE year % 5 = 0 OR year = (SELECT MAX(year) FROM glaciers) ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average ice lost per year in each decade (metres of water equivalent)
queries.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT year, cumulative_mass_balance_mwe - LAG(cumulative_mass_balance_mwe) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS change FROM glaciers) SELECT CAST((year // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(-AVG(change), 2) AS value FROM d WHERE change IS NOT NULL GROUP BY year // 10 ORDER BY year // 10 LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Ice lost each year over the last 20 years (metres of water equivalent)
queries.sql: WITH d AS (SELECT year, cumulative_mass_balance_mwe - LAG(cumulative_mass_balance_mwe) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS change FROM glaciers) SELECT CAST(year AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(-change, 2) AS value FROM d WHERE year > (SELECT MAX(year) FROM glaciers) - 20 ORDER BY year LIMIT 30

story.lead: Glaciers have lost 29.7 metres of ice, faster lately
story.summary: Since 1956, the world's reference glaciers have lost ice equal to **29.7 metres** of water spread over their surface. The yearly loss is now about **five times** what it was in the 1980s: **0.97** metres a year in the 2020s against **0.19**.
story.sub: Average of the world's reference glaciers (WGMS via US EPA), 1956 to 2023; 2020s cover 2020 to 2023 only.

facts.label: Ice lost in 2023, the biggest yearly loss shown

points.h: The total loss keeps climbing, and the climb is steeper
points.p: The line shows ice lost since 1956, in metres of water equivalent, which is the depth of water the melted ice would make. It reached **6** metres by 1980 and **12.9** by 2000. By 2023 it was **29.7**, so more than half of all the loss came after 2000.

points.h: Yearly losses were small until the 1990s, then grew
points.p: In the 1960s, 70s and 80s glaciers lost about **0.2** metres a year. That jumped to **0.48** in the 1990s and has risen every decade since. The 2020s so far average **0.97** metres a year, about **five times** the 1980s.

points.h: The last two years were the biggest losses on record here
points.p: Over the last 20 years, yearly loss ranged from **0.38** metres in 2008 to **1.23** in 2023. Every year since 2015 was at **0.65** or more. 2022 (**1.09**) and 2023 (**1.23**) were the two largest in this period.

story.note: Metres of water equivalent is the depth of water you would get if the lost ice melted, not the thinning of the ice itself.

q: How has the euro moved against the dollar?

queries.purpose: Average euros per US dollar each year since 1999 (higher = stronger dollar; 2026 so far)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(rate), 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Highest and lowest yearly average, to show the range of the swings
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Strongest dollar month (' || strftime(month, '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY rate DESC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Weakest dollar month (' || strftime(month, '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY rate ASC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Latest month (' || strftime(month, '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY month DESC LIMIT 1)

queries.purpose: Monthly euros per US dollar over the last 24 months
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT month AS m, strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(rate, 3) AS value FROM exchange_rates WHERE country = 'Euro' ORDER BY month DESC LIMIT 24) ORDER BY m

story.lead: The euro has gained on the dollar since 2000
story.summary: One US dollar bought **1.117 euros** on average in 2001. In 2026 so far it buys **0.861**, and in September 2026 it bought **0.869**. The big swings ended around 2015, and the rate has stayed in a narrower band since.
story.sub: Monthly euro exchange rates from the US Federal Reserve, January 1999 to September 2026 (2026 is a partial year).

facts.label: bought by one US dollar, Sep 2026
euros per dollar: highest (Oct 2000) and lowest (Jul 2008) months
euros per dollar, Jan 2025 to Sep 2025

points.h: The dollar fell until 2008, then settled in a band
points.p: A dollar bought **1.117 euros** in 2001 but only **0.683** in 2008. It then climbed back to about **0.90** in 2015 and has stayed between roughly **0.85 and 0.95** since. A lower number means a weaker dollar and a stronger euro.

points.h: The biggest gap between months was almost two to one
points.p: The dollar was strongest in October 2000 at **1.173 euros**. It was weakest in July 2008 at **0.635**. That is a swing of nearly **twice** the lower figure. September 2026, at **0.869**, sits between the two extremes.

points.h: The dollar slid in 2025, then held steady
points.p: In January 2025 a dollar bought **0.966 euros**. By September 2025 that was **0.852**. Over the 12 months since, the rate has stayed between **0.846 and 0.875**, with little movement.

story.note: The rate is how many euros one US dollar buys, so a falling number means a weaker dollar. The euro only exists in this data from January 1999.

q: When was the stock market most volatile?

queries.purpose: Highest monthly VIX closes (fear index peaks)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(vix, 1) AS value FROM vix ORDER BY vix DESC LIMIT 12

queries.purpose: Average VIX by year
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(vix), 1) AS value FROM vix WHERE year(month) < 2026 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Average VIX by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year(month) // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(vix), 1) AS value FROM vix GROUP BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 ORDER BY (year(month) // 10) * 10 LIMIT 30

story.lead: Fear peaked in October 2008, during the financial crisis.
story.summary: The stock market's "fear index" (the VIX) hit its highest month-end level in October 2008, at **59.9** points. March 2020 came third at **53.5**. For comparison, a typical calm year averages about **12 to 15**, so the 2008 peak was around four times a quiet reading.
story.sub: Monthly closing VIX, January 1990 to September 2026; yearly averages cover 1990-2019 as shown.

points.h: The three scariest months were 2008 and 2020
points.p: The VIX is a score of how nervous investors are: higher means more fear. **Oct 2008** (**59.9**) and **Nov 2008** (**55.8**) top the list, with **Mar 2020** (**53.5**) third. Eight of the twelve highest months fall in 1998 or in 2008-2009.

points.h: Yearly fear was highest in 2008 and 2009
points.p: Averaged over a full year, 2009 (**31.8**) and 2008 (**31.6**) were the most nervous. The calmest of the years shown was 2017 at **11**. Fear also ran above 23 for most of 1997 to 2002.

points.h: The 2000s were the most nervous decade
points.p: The 2000s averaged **21.9**, the highest of any decade. The 2010s were calmest at **17.1**. The 2020s so far average **20.7**, close to the 2000s.

story.note: The VIX measures how much investors expect the US stock market to swing, using one closing value per month, so a swing within a month can be missed.

q: How have US interest rates changed?

queries.purpose: Average 10-year US government bond yield by decade
queries.sql: SELECT CAST((year(month) // 10) * 10 AS VARCHAR) || 's' AS label, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 2) AS value FROM us_bond_yield GROUP BY (year(month) // 10) ORDER BY (year(month) // 10)

queries.purpose: Average 10-year yield each year since 1990
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 2) AS value FROM us_bond_yield WHERE year(month) >= 1990 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month)

queries.purpose: Highest-yield years on record (annual average)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(yield_pct), 2) AS value FROM us_bond_yield WHERE year(month) < 2026 GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 10

story.lead: US interest rates climbed to 1981, then fell
story.summary: The rate on 10-year US government bonds rose from **3.24%** in the 1950s to **10.59%** in the 1980s. It then fell for 30 years, to **2.41%** in the 2010s. The 2020s so far average **3.1%**, a small rise.
story.sub: US 10-year government bond yield (US Federal Reserve), monthly averages, April 1953 to August 2026.

points.h: Rates rose for 30 years, then fell for 40
points.p: The average yield went up each decade from the 1950s (**3.24%**) to the 1980s (**10.59%**). After that it dropped each decade to **2.41%** in the 2010s. The 2020s average of **3.1%** is the first rise in decades, and it is still well below the 1970s.

points.h: Since 1990, yields slid from 8.55% to about 2%
points.p: The yearly average was **8.55%** in 1990 and **2.14%** in 2019. That is about a quarter of the starting level. The low point was **1.8%** in 2012. The fall was uneven, with small rebounds in 1994, 2006 and 2018.

points.h: The ten highest years were nearly all in the 1980s
points.p: Seven of the ten highest years fall between 1980 and 1985, led by **13.91%** in 1981 and **13%** in 1982. That is more than seven times the 2012 low of **1.8%**. The only other years in the top ten are 1979, 1988, 1989 and 1990, all above **8%**.

story.note: These are yearly or decade averages of monthly values, so single months were higher or lower. The 2020s cover only part of the decade (to August 2026).

q: Which countries have the most people?

queries.purpose: Top 15 countries by population in 2025 (millions of people)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, ROUND(population / 1e6, 1) AS value FROM population WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2025 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Top 15 countries by population in 1960 for comparison (millions of people)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, ROUND(population / 1e6, 1) AS value FROM population WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 1960 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Population growth 1960 to 2025 for the 2025 top 10 countries (millions of extra people)
queries.sql: WITH top AS (SELECT country_code FROM population WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2025 ORDER BY population DESC LIMIT 10) SELECT p25.country AS label, ROUND((p25.population - p60.population) / 1e6, 1) AS value FROM population p25 JOIN population p60 ON p25.country_code = p60.country_code AND p60.year = 1960 WHERE p25.year = 2025 AND p25.country_code IN (SELECT country_code FROM top) ORDER BY value DESC

story.lead: India and China lead, each with over 1.4 billion people.
story.summary: India has the most people, about **1,464 million** (1.46 billion) in 2025, just ahead of China with **1,407 million**. The United States is a distant third at **342 million**, less than a quarter of India's total. In 1960 China was clearly first; India has since passed it.
story.sub: World Bank population figures by country, 2025 compared with 1960.

facts.label: India's population in 2025, the world's largest
People Russia added since 1960, the least of the top 10

points.h: India and China are far ahead of everyone else
points.p: India has **1,463.9 million** people and China **1,406.6 million**. The United States, in third place, has **341.8 million**. Four of the top 15 countries are in Africa, and four more are in South Asia: Pakistan, Bangladesh and India among them.

points.h: In 1960, China led and the list looked different
points.p: China had **667.1 million** people and India **436 million**. Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, France and Ukraine were in the top 15 then. None of them are in the 2025 top 15, while Nigeria and Pakistan are close to the bottom of the 1960 list.

points.h: India added more people than any other country
points.p: India grew by **1,027.9 million** since 1960, more than the whole population of the United States and Brazil put together. China added **739.5 million**. Russia added only **23.6 million**, far less than the rest of the top 10.

story.note: Country names follow the World Bank; figures are for 2025 and 1960, and the 2025 values are as reported in this snapshot.

q: How cheap is natural gas now?

queries.purpose: Recent monthly Henry Hub gas price, last 24 months
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(month, '%b %Y') AS label, ROUND(usd_per_mmbtu, 2) AS value FROM (SELECT month, usd_per_mmbtu FROM gas_prices ORDER BY month DESC LIMIT 24) ORDER BY month

queries.purpose: Average price per year since 1997 for context (2026 so far)
queries.sql: SELECT CAST(year(month) AS VARCHAR) AS label, ROUND(AVG(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) AS value FROM gas_prices GROUP BY year(month) ORDER BY year(month) LIMIT 30

queries.purpose: Latest month compared with the highest-priced years, to show where now sits
queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM (SELECT 'Latest month (' || strftime(MAX(month), '%b %Y') || ')' AS label, ROUND(arg_max(usd_per_mmbtu, month), 2) AS value FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Average since 1997', ROUND(AVG(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Median since 1997', ROUND(median(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Cheapest month ever (' || strftime(arg_min(month, usd_per_mmbtu), '%b %Y') || ')', ROUND(MIN(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices UNION ALL SELECT 'Most expensive month (' || strftime(arg_max(month, usd_per_mmbtu), '%b %Y') || ')', ROUND(MAX(usd_per_mmbtu), 2) FROM gas_prices) ORDER BY value DESC

story.lead: Natural gas is cheaper than usual, but not at a record low.
story.summary: In August 2026, US natural gas cost **$2.78** per million BTU (a standard unit of energy). That is about **a third below** the average of **$4.09** since 1997. It is still almost double the cheapest month ever, **$1.49** in March 2024.
story.sub: Henry Hub spot price (US EIA), monthly, January 1997 to August 2026, in nominal US dollars per million BTU.

facts.label: Price in August 2026, per million BTU

points.h: Prices have settled near $3 after a January spike
points.p: Over the last two years the price mostly moved between **$2** and **$4**. January 2026 jumped to **$7.72**, the highest in this period. By August 2026 it had fallen back to **$2.78**.

points.h: This year's average is higher than 2023 and 2024
points.p: The yearly average in 2026 so far is **$3.61**, above **$2.54** in 2023 and **$2.19** in 2024. That average includes the January spike. It is well below the peaks of **$8.81** in 2005 and **$8.86** in 2008.

points.h: The latest month sits below average, well above the floor
points.p: August 2026's **$2.78** is under both the average (**$4.09**) and the median (**$3.40**). The median is the middle month: half of all months cost more. The all-time low of **$1.49** was about half of today's price.

story.note: Prices are in current US dollars, not adjusted for inflation, so older prices would look higher in today's money. The 2026 average covers January to August only.

q: Which countries have the highest inflation?

queries.purpose: Highest consumer price inflation in 2023 (latest year)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, ROUND(inflation_pct, 1) AS value FROM inflation WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year = 2023 AND inflation_pct IS NOT NULL ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Average inflation 2019-2023 (countries with at least 4 years reported)
queries.sql: SELECT country AS label, ROUND(AVG(inflation_pct), 1) AS value FROM inflation WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND year BETWEEN 2019 AND 2023 AND inflation_pct IS NOT NULL GROUP BY country HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Highest single-year inflation ever recorded, with the year
queries.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT country, year, inflation_pct, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY inflation_pct DESC) AS rn FROM inflation WHERE NOT is_aggregate AND inflation_pct IS NOT NULL) SELECT country || ' (' || CAST(year AS VARCHAR) || ')' AS label, ROUND(inflation_pct, 1) AS value FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

story.lead: Zimbabwe's prices rose fastest, by far.
story.summary: In 2023, Zimbabwe had the highest inflation of any country: prices rose **921.5%** in one year, so they were about ten times higher by the end. That is more than four times the next country, Sudan, at **213.7%**. Zimbabwe also tops the list over 2019–2023, averaging **426.4%** a year.
story.sub: World Bank consumer price data by country: 2023, the 2019–2023 average, and every year since 1961.

points.h: Zimbabwe, Sudan and Argentina led in 2023
points.p: Zimbabwe's prices rose **921.5%** in 2023, far ahead of Sudan (**213.7%**) and Argentina (**135.4%**). Türkiye was fourth at 68.2%. From Ghana down, the rest of the top 15 sit between about 22% and 33%.

points.h: Zimbabwe also leads over the last five years
points.p: Averaged over 2019–2023, Zimbabwe's prices rose **426.4%** a year, and Sudan's **146.7%**. Cuba (**109%**), Lebanon and Syria also averaged close to or above 80% a year. Only countries with at least four years of data are included.

points.h: The worst single years were in the 1980s and 1990s
points.p: The highest yearly rise was in Congo (Dem. Rep.) in 1994: **26,762%**. Georgia in 1993 (**15,444.4%**) and Nicaragua in 1988 (**13,611.6%**) follow. All 15 peaks are far above Zimbabwe's 2023 figure, and none come from after 1996.

story.note: Inflation is the yearly rise in consumer prices; a 100% rise means prices doubled. Some countries may not report every year.

q: Which US cities saw the biggest house price rises?

queries.purpose: Price rise since January 2000 to each city's latest month, top 20 cities
queries.sql: SELECT regexp_replace(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, round(arg_max("index", month) - 100, 0) AS value FROM us_house_prices WHERE regexp_matches(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-') GROUP BY area ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 20

queries.purpose: Price rise over the last 10 years (latest month vs 10 years earlier), top 20 cities
queries.sql: WITH last AS (SELECT area, max(month) AS m FROM us_house_prices WHERE regexp_matches(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-') GROUP BY area) SELECT regexp_replace(l.area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, round((n."index" / o."index" - 1) * 100, 0) AS value FROM last l JOIN us_house_prices n ON n.area = l.area AND n.month = l.m JOIN us_house_prices o ON o.area = l.area AND o.month = l.m - INTERVAL 10 YEAR ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 20

queries.purpose: Price rise over the last 5 years (latest month vs 5 years earlier), top 20 cities
queries.sql: WITH last AS (SELECT area, max(month) AS m FROM us_house_prices WHERE regexp_matches(area, '^[A-Z]{2}-') GROUP BY area) SELECT regexp_replace(l.area, '^[A-Z]{2}-', '') AS label, round((n."index" / o."index" - 1) * 100, 0) AS value FROM last l JOIN us_house_prices n ON n.area = l.area AND n.month = l.m JOIN us_house_prices o ON o.area = l.area AND o.month = l.m - INTERVAL 5 YEAR ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 20

story.lead: Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego led the rises
story.highlight: Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego
story.summary: Since January 2000, home prices in Los Angeles are up **353%**, with Miami (**352%**) and San Diego (**350%**) right behind. That means a typical home in these cities now costs about four and a half times what it did in 2000. Over the last 10 years, Miami leads, with prices up **111%**, so more than doubled.
story.sub: S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller home price index for 20 US metro areas, January 2000 to each city's latest month (June or July 2026); prices not adjusted for inflation.

facts.label: Los Angeles price rise since January 2000
Miami price rise over the last 10 years
Detroit rise since 2000, the smallest of the 20

points.h: Three California and Florida cities top the long-run list
points.p: Los Angeles (**353%**), Miami (**352%**) and San Diego (**350%**) are almost level at the top. Seattle is next at **293%**. At the bottom, Detroit is up **104%**, so prices there have roughly doubled since 2000.

points.h: Over 10 years, Miami and Tampa lead the pack
points.p: Miami is up **111%** over the last decade, ahead of Tampa and Charlotte, both at **105%**. Los Angeles, the long-run leader, is at **82%** here. Even Washington, last on this list, is up **59%**.

points.h: Over 5 years, Miami still leads, but New York and Chicago climb
points.p: Miami is up **49%** in five years, then New York at **46%** and Chicago at **43%**. Cities that led over 10 years, such as Phoenix (**20%**) and Seattle (**15%**), have slowed. San Francisco is lowest at **11%**.

story.note: Figures are percentage rises in the Case-Shiller index, in current dollars, so they include inflation; each city's latest month is June or July 2026.
